newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BOE says further interest rate rises needed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BOE says further interest rate rises needed.

text.p: The Bank of England warned Britain's Conservative government on Wednesday that it was unlikely to meet its 2.5 percent inflation target and would probably have to raise interest rates again.

In its quarterly Inflation Report, the central bank welcomed finance minister Kenneth Clarke's unexpected decision to raise interest rates last week, but made it clear he could not rest on his laurels.
"There is now much less chance of inflation being below 2-1/2 percent during 1997. Achievement of the inflation target remains elusive," it said.

"What matters most is the continuous pursuit of a monetary policy which is consistent with achieving the target in the medium term. To ensure this outcome, some further rise in interest rates is likely to become necessary in due course."
Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, bowed to Bank of England pressure last week after months of resistance and raised official interest rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent.
This was seen as a bold move as British governments are normally reluctant to upset millions of home-owners by pushing up the cost of borrowing in the run-up to a general election.
An election must be held by next May and the Conservatives lag well behind the opposition Labour party in opinion polls.
Wednesday's inflation report suggested there would be no let-up in the pressure on Clarke from the central bank to stick to the path of monetary virtue, despite the looming election.
The Bank's chief economist, Mervyn King, said underlying annual inflation could edge back above 3.0 percent in the next month or so from 2.9 percent in September.
"The Bank is tightening the screws," said Ciaran Barr, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The government welcomed the report and insisted that any differences between it and the Bank were very small.
"The differences between the Treasury and Bank of England on inflation targets are very small and the uncertainties on this type of forecast are very large," a Treasury spokesman said.

Share prices slipped from their day's highs after the report was released as higher interest rates would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money and make other forms of investment more attractive than shares.

The pound fell against the deutschemark and the dollar. Foreign exchage dealers were worried about the prospect of higher inflation and by the Bank's comment that sterling's recent strength was likely to prove temporary.
The Bank said that since its last report in August, the short-run outlook for inflation had deteriorated, sterling's value had risen by nine percent and economic growth had picked up.
Domestic demand, especially consumption, had replaced exports as the main engine of economic growth.
It delivered a veiled warning to the Chancellor not to be tempted into an unduly generous tax giveaway in his last pre-election budget on November 26.
"An appropriate fiscal policy can help to restrain the growth of either public or private consumption," the report said.

"But if monetary policy fails to counter-act the potential inflationary consequences of growth of domestic demand then, as in the late 1980s, the problem could become a weak rather than a strong exchange rate."
